# Struct size check (memory layout demo)

*Generated by qwen3.8-flash*

This example measures how much memory Go structs occupy using
[`unsafe.Sizeof`](https://pkg.go.dev/unsafe#Sizeof) and
[`unsafe.Offsetof`](https://pkg.go.dev/unsafe#Offsetof), inspired by the
[enums example](../enums): how much does a "safe enum" `Color` value cost
compared to a plain `int`?

## Running

```bash
cd struct-size-check
go run .
```

Expected output (amd64 / 64-bit):

```
=== single-value types ===
int                :  8 bytes
color (named int)  :  8 bytes
Color{id color}    :  8 bytes
*Color             :  8 bytes
struct{} (empty)   :  0 bytes

=== structs grow with fields ===
ColorNamed{id; name}: 24 bytes (color=8 + string=16, no padding)
  offset of .name   :  8 bytes
Padded{b bool; i int64}: 16 bytes (1 + 7 padding + 8)
  offset of .i      :  8 bytes

=== collections ===
[4]Color  : 32 bytes (4 * 8)
[]Color   : 24 bytes for the slice header (ptr+len+cap), data is on the heap
```

On a 32-bit platform (`GOARCH=386`) all pointer/int sizes halve:
`go env GOARCH` shows the current one.

## What it shows

1. **A named type is not a wrapper.** `type color int` has exactly the same
   size and alignment as `int` — the type name only exists at compile time.

2. **A single-field struct costs the same as its field.** `Color{id color}`
   is 8 bytes, just like a plain `int`. Struct size = sum of field sizes
   plus alignment padding; with one field there is no padding. So the enum
   emulation in [`enums/colors/colors.go`](../enums/colors/colors.go) is
   **free at runtime** — the safety is enforced by the compiler.

3. **Fields make structs grow.** Adding a `string` field (`ColorNamed`)
   jumps the size to 24 bytes: 8 (`color`) + 16 (string header = pointer +
   length), no padding needed because both parts are 8-byte aligned.

4. **Alignment padding is real.** `Padded{b bool; i int64}` costs 16 bytes,
   not 9: the compiler inserts 7 padding bytes after `bool` so that `int64`
   starts at an 8-byte offset (`unsafe.Offsetof` shows the gap). Reordering
   fields (`i` first, then `b`) keeps it at 16, but packing several small
   bools around large fields matters in big structs.

5. **Arrays vs slices.** `[4]Color` is 32 bytes of contiguous data; a
   `[]Color` itself is only the 24-byte header (ptr/len/cap), the elements
   live on the heap.

## Verification

```bash
cd struct_size_check
go vet ./...
go build ./...
```
